The study was conducted by the McDonnell Aircraft Company under Air Force Contract F33615-78-C-3140.
Hercules AS/3501-6 and Narmco T300/5208 graphite-epoxy materials were used to fabricate the test specimens.
The baseline laminate configuration was a 50/40/10 layup of 0°, ±45°, and 90° plies.
Specimen thicknesses ranged from 20 to 60 plies, with hole sizes from 0.1870 to 0.4995 inches.
The double shear test setup was used for most static strength tests, with load-deflection data obtained from an externally mounted compliance gage.
Moisture preconditioning of specimens involved a multi-phase exposure to 95% RH at 180°F, followed by 55% RH to achieve an equilibrium moisture content of 0.86%.
Failure modes observed in the static tests included bearing, bearing-shearout, shearout-tension-cleavage, and net section failures.
Task 3 evaluated the effects of anomalies such as hole drilling defects, porosity, and interference fit variations on joint strength.
Task 4 fatigue tests were conducted under both constant amplitude and spectrum loading conditions, with environmental exposure.
Fatigue life data was obtained for the critical design variables and manufacturing anomalies identified from the Task 2 and 3 strength tests.
The study resulted in over 400 static and fatigue tests to develop improved methods for predicting the strength and durability of bolted composite joints.
The test data and analysis from this study were used to develop the Bolted Joint Stress Field Model (BJSFM) computer program, documented in Volume 3 of the report.
The research program was conducted from February 1978 to April 1981 under the Air Force's Structural Mechanics project.
The work was performed by the McDonnell Aircraft Company, a division of the McDonnell Douglas Corporation, located in St. Louis, Missouri.
The Air Force project engineers were Mr. Roger J. Aschenbrenner and Capt. Robert L. Gallo from the Air Force Wright Aeronautical Laboratories.
